title: The Poisoned Wife cold case and a private eye who won’t give up
transcript:
Speaker 1: From The Australian, here's what's on the front. I'm Claire Harvey. It's Monday, November 23, 2026. Anthony Albanese is one of the least trusted or liked Prime Ministers in recent history. That's according to an exclusive news poll in The Australian Today, which shows 64% of Australians are dissatisfied with the PM and he's behind opposition leader Angus Taylor as preferred Prime Minister. That's an exclusive live now at theaustralian.com.au. Rosalind McQueen was 30 years old, pregnant and looking forward to the birth of her second child, a baby boy, when she died an horrific death by strychnine poisoning in the Victorian countryside in 1986. Her toddler, Jodie, was found next to Ros's dead body in the family home. 40 years on, the Poisoned Wife podcast has rocketed to the top of charts around the world, bringing Roz's story to light. Today, our national chief correspondent, Hedley Thomas, is here to reveal how new evidence laws could solve this crime.
Speaker 2: I want to know whether you can help bring a cold case to a close. I found the death of Rosalind McQueen near Bendigo was carefully planned. And to this day, her killer walks free.
Speaker 1: Hedley Thomas is the Australian's national chief correspondent. And if you love podcasts, you will be deep in The Poisoned Wife, Hedley's 2026 piece of work about the death of a mother and the unsolved murder of Rosalind McQueen in Victoria in the 1980s. Hedley, you often acquire a storytelling partner in these podcasts. In The Poisoned Wife, it's a septuagenarian private detective retired called Rex. How did Rex come into your life?
Speaker 3: Oh, my God. Rex Bakes, he's a national treasure. And the first time I heard from him, he telephoned me. Somehow he'd got my mobile phone and I was exhausted. It was a public holiday. I was having a glass of wine at home with Ruth and and just feeling relieved that I had a bit of time off. And this guy just starts talking, you know, a hundred words a minute about this case that he's obsessed by and wants me to get involved in it. I know I was brusque with him. I think I just told him, not now, mate, you know, send me an email. But I didn't realize Rex Bakes doesn't do email. He's never had internet connectivity. He doesn't even use a mobile phone. So that was a completely forlorn gesture. He ended up writing me numerous letters. And I've received two more this week.
Speaker 4: Wow.
Speaker 3: They're all handwritten. And they have his ideas about the unsolved murder of Ros McQueen. And since he knows this series is coming to an end, he's now suggesting all these other cold cases that as a private investigator, he's known about. But the catalyst for me to get involved in The Poisoned Wife and to go on the road with Rex Bakes across regional Victoria was the suitcase. Rex went to an op shop in the country town of Barmera in South Australia, where he lives, and bought this old suitcase, filled it with all these documents that he had collected over years of his own investigations into Ross McQueen's death, and he sent it to me. with padlocks on it and a separate envelope with the key to open the locks. It's going to get your attention.
Speaker 1: Calling the bomb squad. Yeah.
Speaker 3: Sarah Elks was pretty concerned in the Brisbane Bureau when it turned up. And that was four years ago. It was right after the conviction of Chris Dawson. Convicted murderer Chris Dawson will wake up this morning in a small concrete prison cell after he was found guilty of killing his first wife Lynette 40 years ago. And he thought, I want this guy to help me investigate Roz's death. Rex was also unwell. He had cancer. He was concerned that he would, as he calls it, end up soon on Boot Hill and he needed a sidekick. This suitcase of material that you've sent to me, these thousands of documents.
Speaker 4: Every single piece of paper I got about this case, you have now got.
Speaker 3: And when you have someone like Rex Bakes coming out of the woodwork with his trilby hat on and with all of his old school trays and ways, you think, I've got this amazingly committed elderly man who never knew Ros McQueen. who has this years-long commitment to trying to find her murderer and have him charged. And he's been doing it on his own. And the letters that he's written, which we have, not just to me, he's been writing to government agencies for many years, imploring them to do something. And You can imagine what public servants make of this. They probably want to get this off their desk as quickly as possible. Who gets handwritten letters these days? But Rex has got this saying, the shortest pencil is better than the longest memory. You can forget something really quickly, but if you write it down with the shortest pencil... that's going to be there forever.
Speaker 1: It's also the most compelling evidence, isn't it? Contemporaneous evidence of something is something that courts hold very valuable. If you've written a diary note or you've written a letter back at the time that you saw or heard something, that's evidence that courts absolutely love. Rex is not some crank though. And I felt a bit angry, I think, listening to some of the episodes of The Poisoned Wife when Rex, for example, had been trying to get the transcripts of the coronial proceedings in Rosalind McQueen's case. And just to recap briefly, she died on the 1st of April 1986. She was poisoned by strychnine. There wasn't a proper police investigation at the time. Her husband, Ray McQueen, was charged with murder. He's always denied any wrongdoing, but the trial never proceeded. So it's just kind of hung there for 40 years.
Speaker 3: And the coroner determined that he did it.
Speaker 5: That's right.
Speaker 1: But when Rex was trying to get those coronial transcripts, They weren't available to him. You and Karina Berger, your journalistic partner on this story, did obtain those transcripts and they've been very useful. I mean, it's outrageous that the proceedings of a public court wouldn't be available to someone like Rex, who's actually the expert here.
Speaker 3: Yeah, we're puzzled over that because Rex was told that those records couldn't be located. And we were wondering, well, how is that possible? Because we were then able to locate them and we had really good cooperation with from Victoria's state coroner who reviewed the matter and also, with the blessing of Victoria Police, released the old brief of evidence that was part of the inquest that unfolded in 1987. But Rex was denied access to it when he asked. And I think there's a real difficulty for decision makers in some of these agencies, particularly in the coroner's court and elsewhere. Where do they draw the line in terms of the release of material. You and I, having been schooled in freedom of information and the public's right to know, we take the view, I'm sure you're on the same page as me, that members of the public have a right to the documents generated through public inquiries.
Speaker 1: Yeah, they're paying for it.
Speaker 3: Yeah. But there's the alternative view, which is, well, there's privacy issues. There's issues around whether the person who's seeking the documentation is Is a legitimate investigator, is that person potentially a crank who's going to make life difficult for next of kin? There are different considerations. I still think that the default should be release unless there are really good reasons not to.
Speaker 1: I think all proceedings should be open. I think not only journalists but members of the public have a right generally to be inside court proceedings. There's a very worrying trend now towards suppression of all names and of witnesses in, say, murder trials. Routinely now, every witness will get a pseudonym at the start of a murder trial. I heard a judge recently at the start of a trial say, well, once upon a time, this person's evidence, they're just an eyewitness to something, would have been reported on for a couple of days in the newspaper, but then we would have all moved on. If I don't give this person a pseudonym, their name will be associated with this alleged crime forever, even though they're kind of only a bit player in it. I mean, I think the courts are paid for by taxpayers. We absolutely have to have the public's right to know what is going on. And that has to endure, I think, that right too. I mean, I think it matters if someone comes and gives evidence in a court. One of the things, apart from the oath, that makes you tell the truth is the knowledge that this is public.
Speaker 3: Yeah, I think it's a really poor approach. And it shows how high-handed some judicial officers think they should be or can be. Consider the situation where, if, for example, that case, that trial collapsed before a verdict or ended with, say, an acquittal, and then years later, an investigative journalist or a member of the family decided to do their own investigations and research, but they couldn't really take it far at all because all the records were didn't indicate who the witnesses were. So they couldn't go back, follow up, and check information facts with the witnesses because they've all got pseudonyms. Because a judge has decided in his or her high-handed way that they're going to effectively censor the public record. That's outrageous. Why isn't that being challenged? That should not stand. I agree.
Speaker 1: Rex was a private investigator who was originally hired by the defence, by the accused killer's defence team, to try and help prove his innocence. Rex took a different view and believes that, in fact, there could still be a conviction in this matter if it was taken back to trial.
Speaker 4: I'm really, really annoyed with Victoria Police. This case is easily solvable. They're just not interested.
Speaker 1: If I was Victoria Police, I would be all over you trying to get be documents that you have, presumably which they don't have anymore, I don't know. What's happening in regard to that?
Speaker 3: It seems Victoria Police have effectively given up on this case. They believe that it's too old. You know, there was a powerful circumstantial case that was put together by a detective called Ron Blackshaw. And, you know, Ron is a man now in his early 80s, lives on the Sunshine Coast, has been a great help, along with Rex Bakes, in this investigation for the poisoned wife. And Ron is the sort of guy who would normally run away from, I think, media attention. But, you know, he very kindly agreed to be interviewed several times for the series and to review a lot of the work that he had done in putting together this brief in 1986 and 1987. And, you know, he has held out hope that all these years later it could still be solved. So you'd never rule it out. We'd need to get, though, a witness who comes forward with the smoking jar.
Speaker 1: Yeah.
Speaker 4: Yeah.
Speaker 1: That seems like a very high bar for a 40-year-old case. In the Chris Dawson matter, it was a judge-alone trial. The judge found that Dawson, even though that was also a circumstantial case, had murdered his wife, Lynn Sims.
Speaker 2: Christopher Michael Dawson on the charge that on about 8 January 1982 at Bayview.
Speaker 2: Or elsewhere in the state of New South Wales, you did murder Lynette Dawson.
Speaker 4: I find you guilty. You may sit down.
Speaker 1: Chris Dawson's now in jail. This fails on appeals. I mean, it seems that we have a new understanding now of what violence against women looks like or what family violence looks like. Again, Ray McQueen has always pleaded not guilty. If it went to trial, he would have the right to a defence and he might be acquitted. But I think it's worth giving it a go, isn't it?
Speaker 3: Well, it should be. And one of the really interesting features of a later episode of The Poisoned Wife is the information that we glean from a very senior former Crown prosecutor from Victoria, who's also done a lot of criminal defense lawyering. And he makes the point that evidence that was excluded in 1987 from the Crown's case in relation to Ray McQueen, leading to ultimately the decision by the DPP to enter a nolle prosequi, basically to discontinue the trial. It's not an exoneration, but it means that the trial doesn't proceed. This barrister, Gavin Silbert, senior counsel, said that in a modern day trial, that the evidence, or a lot of it that was excluded, would almost certainly be allowed in. And the system has evolved. And unfortunately, Ros McQueen's death occurred at a time when it could be challenged and excluded.
Speaker 1: You've made your storytelling work in audio about violence against women, family violence, women who've been murdered. Earlier this year, Pauline Hanson, who was having a bit of a moment herself this year, said that she didn't really understand why women in violent situations didn't just leave.
Speaker 5: I just feel that if you're not in a house where you feel safe, you don't want to be there, then you shouldn't put up with it. And if these women are getting abused by men out there, then don't put up with it. That's what I'm saying.
Speaker 1: I mean, that is the oldest kind of argument in the book, isn't it? I thought we were past that. What did you think hearing that?
Speaker 3: I think it's a very foolish, short-sighted, comment to make. It belies ignorance of the circumstances of how women are prepared to tough things out for the sake of children, family, to try to make something work, even when they must suspect they're living with a monster. But a lot of women don't know that their husband may be plotting to kill them. They're in a domestically violent relationship. And They're prepared to take that because the alternative for a lot of them looks worse. It looks intolerable.
Speaker 1: And also their confidence has been shattered. They might have lost connection to their family or, you know, anywhere to go.
Speaker 3: Yeah. So it's, you know, I think an archaic and ignorant statement to make.
Speaker 1: Overall, do you feel as though Australia is getting better at this? We hear often kind of a bit of a dystopian sense that domestic violence is at an epidemic and it's all kind of much worse than it was. I actually wonder if it's always been pretty bad, but now we're just hearing about it more. What do you think?
Speaker 3: I think, like you, the latter. I'm sure that it's not necessarily improving in great leaps and bounds, but scrutiny of it and condemnation of it and transparency around it is a lot different. And we're prepared to talk about it more. And thankfully, organizations exist to help women in this situation with much more resources and effort and commitment than in the past. I think also that journalists and media outlets are playing a significant part in this, publicizing it, campaigning against it. That must have a deterrent factor. But if a male who is predisposed to violence just loses it, and has a red mist. All of the deterrents in the world, all of the campaigns that he may have witnessed in the past is not going to make a scrap of difference, I suspect. It's just a rage that is primitive, uncontrolled, and is going to lead to a terrible situation. And you just hope, and this is what I think a lot of women get out of ours and other podcast investigations, they identify in these stories risk factors that And, you know, a lot of women tell me this is why they listen, because they're worried in their own situation or they're worried for friends and loved ones in their situations. And by informing themselves, by listening to the characterizations of dangerous males, they're better equipped and they feel like they can then make decisions that are in their best interests and could keep them safe.
Speaker 1: Hedley, thank you very much.
Speaker 4: Thanks, Claire.
Speaker 1: Hedley Thomas is The Australian's National Chief Correspondent and creator of The Poisoned Wife podcast. Subscribers can hear all episodes now at thepoisonedwife.com, on The Australian's app and on Apple Podcasts. Just search The Poisoned Wife.
